name: PT Map Boga Adiperkasa Tbk

frontmatter.title: Map Boga Adiperkasa: the recovery is real, the price already assumes it
frontmatter.summary: The Starbucks licensee in Indonesia is recovering sales, and on our corrected cost path the operating margin returns to the FY2023 structure by FY2030E. Even so, a DCF struck after the full rent values the equity at Rp950 against a Rp1,115 price, and the thickest part of the value sits in a terminal period the company has never earned. SELL.
thesis: Sales are recovering, profit is not yet: 9M2026 sales rose at a high single-digit rate while the operating loss held flat, because gross margin fell and costs grew almost as fast [S3].

The lease book is the real cost. Lease payments absorbed most of operating cash flow in FY2025, leaving free cash flow to equity negative once capex is paid [S2]. Our DCF charges that rent in full and bridges the equity on net cash, because the lease is an operating cost, not debt.

The base case does return close to the FY2023 cost structure by FY2030E - marginally above it, not below, and we no longer assume a structural cost reset - but the value that produces still sits below the market price: 77.7% of it is terminal and the near years are loss-making.
The multiple the market pays looks modest only because it is struck on a rent-free EBITDA, and the peer median is almost exactly the multiple already applied to this name [S0].

A register held mostly by insiders, a free float of 7.88% — above the minimum in force but below the fifteen per cent the exchange has proposed [S9] — and negligible traded value make the shares effectively uninvestable at size, which the house liquidity rule applies in the target [S0, S3].
The licence is the asset that matters; the LK discloses royalty-bearing brand agreements without a rate or a term, which is the largest unquantified risk and is carried in the bear case [S2].

catalysts.event: Q4 2026 trading and full-year store count; whether the sales recovery holds through the holiday quarter
FY2026 audited results: gross margin and the operating loss are the two lines that matter
Any AGM resolution on the free float or further non-preemptive issuance

blocks.text: **SELL, target Rp711 (-36.3% versus Rp1,115).** MAP Boga Adiperkasa operates the Starbucks franchise in Indonesia, alongside a small portfolio of other licensed food and beverage brands, and it is a subsidiary of the Mitra Adiperkasa retail group [S2]. It is a good business in a bad patch, and the shares are priced as if the patch is already behind it.

The demand story is a genuine rebound. Nine-month sales of IDR2,566.8bn compare with IDR2,354.4bn a year earlier [S3], and the estate has stopped shrinking at 592 Starbucks stores [S4]. The problem is that the rebound has not reached the profit line. Gross profit rose to IDR1,735.7bn, but selling and administrative costs rose almost as much, and the operating loss was essentially unchanged [S3]. Management has cut the cost base hard since the downturn — FY2025 revenue of IDR3,236.0bn against a peak of IDR3,999.5bn in FY2023 [S0] — but each additional rupiah of sales currently arrives at close to zero incremental operating profit [S2, S3].

The cash flow makes the point more sharply than the income statement. Operating cash flow of IDR401.7bn in FY2025 was more than consumed by capex of IDR130.0bn and lease payments of IDR311.7bn, and cash fell over the year to IDR376.0bn [S2]. We model the business after that rent, not before it: the lease is an operating cost paid to landlords, the D&A add-back nets the lease charge out of the cash flow, and the lease liability is not deducted again in the bridge. MAPB has no bank debt [S2], so on this basis the equity is bridged on net cash.

Our value rests on a DCF in which the recovery continues and the cost ratio unwinds toward the level the estate has already earned. Revenue compounds from IDR3,501.4bn to IDR4,378.6bn, gross margin recovers to 69.5%, the operating cost ratio falls to 64.8% of sales — marginally above the FY2023 ratio, not below it — and EBIT reaches IDR205.8bn by the final forecast year [S0, S3]. That is a real recovery, not a straw man. The equity value it produces is Rp950 per share, below the market price, and 77.7% of that value sits in the terminal period. On the reverse DCF, today's price needs revenue growth of 8.9% a year, sustained, on our cost structure — above the pace we forecast beyond the rebound year.

What would make us wrong is a faster margin recovery than even our restated base case assumes: if the gross-margin compression of 9M2026 reverses while the cost ratio keeps improving at the pace seen in that period, the business earns more than we forecast and the equity is worth materially more. That is the bull case, and we give it real weight. It is not our base case, because the 9M2026 evidence — more sales, no more profit — points the other way.

Premium coffee retail is a scale business: brand, site quality and supply chain determine unit
economics, and rent is usually the largest controllable cost after labour. Where a global brand is
operated by a local licensee, the licensee carries the capital and the rent while the brand owner
collects royalties and retains the right to change partners at renewal. That structure concentrates
risk in the party with the least bargaining power.

MAPB is the Indonesian operator of Starbucks and a portfolio of other licensed food and beverage brands, reporting through beverages, foods and other segments [S2]. The company belongs to the Mitra Adiperkasa group: PT Mitra Adiperkasa Tbk is the majority shareholder and PT Satya Mulia Gema Gemilang is the ultimate shareholder [S2]. It is a licensee, not a brand owner, and that single fact governs the whole investment case.

The brand agreements require the group to pay royalties or fees set in each agreement, and several require it to buy goods from the rights holder or approved vendors; the LK states the obligation exists but discloses neither the rate nor the expiry [S2]. A subsidiary also pays the parent a management fee covering information technology, finance, human resources, supply chain, procurement, internal audit and other corporate services, booked within general and administrative expense [S2]. Store and office leases run from one to ten years with renewal by mutual agreement, contracted with both third parties and related parties [S2]. That combination — royalty to the brand owner, management fee to the parent, rent to landlords — defines the cost stack and explains why a gross margin of 69.1% produces a negative operating result.

The store estate is the operating asset and the growth engine, and it has stopped growing. Indonesia had 592 Starbucks stores at Q3 2026, the tenth-largest market globally and -17 stores versus Q3 2024 [S4]. On FY2025 sales of IDR3,236.0bn that implies modest revenue per store, and the estate was built when volumes were higher. Other brands in the portfolio — the bakery, pizza, doughnut and sushi concepts named in the company's own description — are small beside the coffee business and are not separately disclosed, so we do not attribute value to them beyond the group multiple.

The strategy is defensive rather than expansive: hold the store count, protect the brand's premium position, and let cost control and the sales recovery do the work. Nothing in the filings suggests a return to aggressive new-store openings; capex of IDR130.0bn in FY2025 was a fraction of the expansion years [S2]. For a licensee with a fixed royalty and a lease book, that is the right posture, and it caps the upside: without new stores, revenue growth has to come from like-for-like traffic and price in a category that is itself growing quickly [S8].

The category is growing quickly. Bank Indonesia put the revenue potential of the national coffee industry at IDR222,810.0bn in June 2026, with the number of coffee outlets growing 23.9% a year [S8]. The outlets are being added mainly by local value and mid-market chains, but an outlet-growth statistic says nothing directly about market share, and MAPB discloses neither traffic nor like-for-like sales. The evidence we can source on its own position is that the Indonesian Starbucks estate has shrunk over the past two years while national outlet counts expanded [S4, S8]. We treat the share-shift reading as inference from those two facts, not as a disclosed measure.

Two external forces matter. First, the brand has been exposed to consumer boycotts tied to its US parent. The strongest evidence we have is Korean, not Indonesian: after a May 2026 controversy Starbucks Korea's card-payment volume dropped sharply in the first week, then partially recovered but stayed below its pre-incident level, and the company temporarily closed a large part of the estate for staff training [S7]. We use it as an analogue for how fast a brand-level political shock can remove traffic, not as a measurement of Indonesian demand, and we have found no MAPB traffic disclosure that would settle the question either way. Second, the global parent is restructuring: it announced a round of North American store closures and cut its planned global openings, part of a turnaround programme under its current chief executive [S6]. A parent retrenching globally has less appetite to subsidise a sub-scale licensee and more reason to revisit licence terms at renewal. The LK discloses that royalty-bearing brand agreements exist but not their rate or expiry [S2], so we cannot date that risk; we treat it as the largest unquantified exposure in the name and carry a royalty step in the bear case.

Competitively, the moat is the brand and the real-estate portfolio, not the product. The premium brand's pricing power has visibly weakened — gross margin fell even as sales recovered [S3]. The cause of that fall is our inference, not a disclosed attribution: the LK does not explain its gross margin, and the plausible drivers — imported green coffee and dairy against a weaker rupiah, and deeper discounting to hold traffic — are consistent with the 9M2026 numbers but are not separately quantified in the accounts [S3]. On the five-forces view, buyer power is high in a fragmented category with abundant substitutes, landlord power is high in prime sites, and supplier power is concentrated in the brand owner through the royalty and approved-vendor arrangements [S2]. Only the brand itself, and the habit of its loyal customers, stands against those forces.

Demand is a function of urban disposable income and habit, and both are under pressure. The category's outlet growth [S8] tells us consumers still want coffee; it does not tell us they want to pay a premium for it. In a market where a comparable cup is available at a lower price from a local chain, the premium brand has to earn its price differential every day through service, product and location. The 9M2026 gross margin suggests that, at current price points, it is discounting to hold traffic rather than earning that differential [S3]. That is the mechanism behind the whole thesis: a growing category, a strong brand, and a unit economic that is being competed away at the margin.

Regulation is a secondary influence rather than a primary one: the group operates under Indonesian consumer-protection, labour and tax rules and the exchange's free-float requirements, where the company clears the minimum now in force by a narrow margin but sits far below the fifteen per cent the exchange has proposed [S9]. Macro matters more. Coffee and dairy are imported, so a weaker rupiah raises input costs against sticky menu prices; the macro desk's rupiah path is a headwind for gross margin, and the 9M2026 accounts already show it [S3]. Conversely, the categories the company sells into are consumer-discretionary, and the macro desk's aversion to Indonesian rate-sensitive and discretionary names applies with force here.

Our read on competitive positioning is that MAPB is a strong brand in a weakening position. It remains the reference point for premium coffee in Indonesia and the tenth-largest Starbucks market in the world [S4], which is not a franchise in terminal decline. But the estate is shrinking, the brand owner has alternatives, and the pricing differential is being competed away [S3, S4]. That combination supports a valuation anchored on current economics with an option on recovery, not one that capitalises the recovery as if it were already achieved.

A note on the EBITDA line, because the columns are not on one basis. FY2024A and FY2025A are the reported figure, struck before rent; from FY2026E the table is struck after the full cash rent the DCF charges. The step at FY2026E is that convention, not an operating collapse: FY2025A reported EBITDA of IDR425.9bn less lease payments of IDR311.7bn is the after-rent number that is comparable with the forecast columns [S2].

The five-year record is one of a business that lost its operating leverage. Revenue peaked in FY2023 at IDR3,999.5bn and fell sharply in FY2024; FY2025 sales of IDR3,236.0bn were flat year on year [S0, S2]. Gross margin held at 69.1% through FY2025 — IDR2,235.7bn of gross profit — but selling expenses of IDR2,075.3bn plus administrative costs of IDR297.8bn exceeded it, and finance costs of IDR35.3bn completed the gap to a pre-tax loss [S2]. The company has now posted losses for consecutive years, and equity has fallen from IDR1,686.8bn to IDR1,397.2bn [S0].

The fall from a positive operating margin in FY2023 to a loss in FY2025 is a story about fixed costs on a smaller revenue base, not about a new cost that arrived: opex was IDR2,571.5bn on revenue of IDR3,999.5bn in FY2023, and IDR2,355.2bn on IDR3,236.0bn in FY2025 — roughly the same absolute cost base, on a fifth less revenue [S0]. That is why the base case now returns toward the FY2023 cost structure as revenue recovers, rather than assuming the ratio stays where the downturn put it, and why we do not assume a structural cost reset the LK does not show.

The 9M2026 comparative is the most informative disclosure in the file. Sales rose at a high single-digit rate to IDR2,566.8bn and gross profit rose to IDR1,735.7bn, but the operating loss was essentially unchanged: the incremental revenue arrived at a gross margin roughly two points lower than the prior year, and operating costs grew almost as fast as sales [S3]. The net loss widened to IDR-157.5bn for two reasons that flatter neither the base nor the comparison — the prior period carried a tax benefit that did not repeat, and a foreign-exchange loss hit the current period [S3]. Strip those out and the underlying deterioration is modest; it is still deterioration.

Cash generation is the crux. Operating cash flow of IDR401.7bn looks healthy until the lease book is charged: lease payments including interest were IDR311.7bn and capex IDR130.0bn, so free cash flow to equity was negative and cash fell to IDR376.0bn [S2]. The balance sheet has no bank borrowings — lease liabilities were IDR504.1bn at the last audited year-end and IDR201.4bn of them were due within a year at 30 September 2026 [S2, S3] — and working capital is negative because customers prepay through stored-value cards and suppliers are paid on terms [S3]. Liquidity is adequate for the next twelve months but not generous, and there is no dividend [S0].

Capital allocation has been conservative by necessity. With no bank debt and a lease book that has to be serviced before shareholders, the group has prioritised liquidity over growth: capex fell to IDR130.0bn in FY2025, the dividend is nil, and the 2023 non-preemptive placement was used to strengthen the balance sheet rather than to fund expansion [S2, S5]. That is the right call for a business in this position, but it means there is no financial buffer to absorb another bad year beyond the cash balance and undrawn trade lines [S2]. The balance sheet is not levered in the conventional sense; it is levered to its landlords, and those obligations are contractual and do not flex with sales.

Our forecast puts FY2026E at the 9M2026 run-rate carried through a seasonally stronger fourth quarter. One definitional point first, because it governs every comparison that follows: IDR-119.6bn for FY2025 is the data pack's EBIT, whose operating-cost line is struck net of other operating income, while the LK's own operating result — gross profit of IDR2,235.7bn less selling costs of IDR2,075.3bn and administrative costs of IDR297.8bn — is lower by that item [S2]. Our forecast EBIT is revenue times (gross margin less the operating-cost ratio), which is the pure operating result on the LK's definition. On that definition FY2026E EBIT of IDR-119.0bn is an improvement on the FY2025 operating result, not a flat year: the higher revenue base earns positive incremental gross profit while the cost ratio holds near the 9M2026 level. That improvement is smaller than the 9M2026 sales growth alone would deliver, and it is the honest read of a period in which sales rose and the loss did not fall. From FY2027E the cost ratio unwinds at about two-thirds of the pace measured in 9M2026, gross margin recovers to 69.5%, and EBIT reaches IDR205.8bn (4.7% margin) by FY2030E. We do not forecast a dividend; none has been paid and the losses make one remote [S2].

Earnings-quality flags. There is no accruals problem of the usual kind: cash conversion is honest and the losses are real, with operating cash flow above net income because depreciation and right-of-use amortisation are large non-cash charges. The flags that matter are structural. First, reported EBITDA is not a cash measure here: right-of-use amortisation sits in operating costs while the cash lease payment sits in financing, so we strike FCFF after the full cash rent and add back only total D&A less that rent — the D&A step in FY2026E is a basis change, explained in the valuation section, not a collapse in profitability. Second, the 2023 non-preemptive placement raised fresh capital explicitly to strengthen the balance sheet, diluting minorities without offering them the shares [S5]. Third, related-party flows are disclosed and, relative to the size of the business, small — but they are real levers and we can size most of them. The management fee paid to the parent for shared services was IDR66.5bn in 9M2026 on sales of IDR2,566.8bn, roughly two and a half per cent of revenue, with other payables to related parties of IDR15.8bn covering management fees, leases and advances [S3]. On the audited year-end, trade receivables from related parties — sales settled through the group's own retail outlets — were IDR19.1bn against total assets of IDR2,817.1bn, and board remuneration was IDR27.1bn [S2]. The notes state that no single customer or supplier exceeds a tenth of sales or purchases [S2], so no single related party dominates the P&L. On the contract above, these are optics-class flags, not manipulation-class: disclosed, recurring, and modest against revenue and assets, but struck with a parent on both sides of the table and never benchmarked.

Exchange status is part of the same check: we looked for a special monitoring board designation and for any of the B/E/L/M/S notation letters in the audited and interim filings and the press archived for this note, and found none, and the directors state a going-concern basis with adequate resources [S2, S3]. That is a check of the archived record, not a live exchange screen.

A discounted cash flow is the right primary method for a lease-heavy operator whose earnings are temporarily negative: a P/E is meaningless on a loss, and an EV/EBITDA multiple on a depressed EBITDA embeds the very recovery we are trying to test. We use a WACC of 11.9%, inside the house band for rupiah cash flows, built from a cost of equity of 12.6%, a risk-free rate of 7.4% and a lease-debt weight of 14.1%. That weight needs a word, because the model charges rent in full: it lowers WACC, but the same lease liability is what relevers the beta to 1.02 from an unlevered 0.90, which is what lifts the cost of equity to 12.6%. The two effects offset but not exactly: a consistent no-debt build — the lease weight at zero and the unlevered beta against the same risk-free rate and equity risk premium — gives roughly twelve point zero per cent against the 11.9% used here, about sixteen basis points higher. The cost of that is real but small: close to one and a half per cent of equity, or roughly fifteen rupiah a share, which would leave the target near six hundred and ninety-six rupiah. The stored build is kept because the cash-flow definition and the bridge are the post-rent ones either way, and on the no-debt rate the call is still SELL. The DCF gives Rp950 per share, with 77.7% of the value in the terminal period — high, but unavoidable when the near years are loss-making, and the reason we normalise terminal capex below.

**One lease convention, applied everywhere.** FCFF is struck after the full cash rent: lease payments of IDR311.7bn in FY2025 against a total D&A charge well above them [S0], so the add-back is total D&A less the rent and right-of-use amortisation is never added back, because it is the rent. Two consequences follow, and both are in the model. First, the lease liability is not deducted in the bridge: the after-rent cash flow has already paid it, and deducting the IDR504.1bn lease book a second time would charge rent twice against the same cash flow. MAPB has no bank debt [S2], so the DCF is bridged on net cash, with the lease liability listed as a bridge item so the arithmetic is visible on the page. Second, the lease-interest element of the rent (IDR35.3bn in FY2025 [S2]) sits below EBIT in the LK and is netted out inside the D&A add-back, so the whole occupancy cost is charged exactly once. The multiple cross-check cannot be put on the same basis: every EV/EBITDA multiple available to us is a pre-rent, lease-as-debt measure, so we show it and do not weight it.

The terminal value is the weak point of any DCF of this business, and we have stopped it leaning on asset consumption. In the draft the red team saw, FY2030E capex sat below that year's D&A add-back, so most of the terminal cash flow was the estate being run down while the model assumed perpetual growth. Capex now ramps to 7.3% of sales — IDR319.6bn against an add-back of IDR308.7bn — so terminal capex exceeds the D&A charge and the terminal value is earned rather than harvested. Growth of 4.0% on FY2030E EBIT of IDR205.8bn implies an exit value below the 6.6x the market pays today on EBITDA: no multiple expansion is being capitalised, which is the test this kind of DCF usually fails.

The cross-check argues the other way, and it is circular. Our own table of the ten Indonesian leisure and restaurant names in the coverage universe — CNMA, ENAK, GOLF, HRME, JSPT, KOTA, PJAA, PTSP, PZZA and SHID — carries a median EV/EBITDA that sits within a whisker of the multiple the market already applies to MAPB's own rent-free EBITDA of 6.6x [S0]. The median is our own computation from those ten names, not a third-party estimate, and the multiple on the right is the data pack's; that they coincide is what "peer median" means in a sector where the comparison set is the market itself. Converted to this company's lease intensity, the same multiple implies a far higher multiple on after-rent EBITDA, a rating no shrinking, loss-making estate earns. We therefore report the multiple as a cross-check, explain the basis gap, and give it no weight in the target; the DCF carries the valuation and the reverse DCF below tests it from the other side.

What today's price implies. Running our own cost structure backwards, Rp1,115 requires revenue growth of about 8.9% a year, sustained, to justify the price on the DCF. That is the pace of the current cyclical rebound extended indefinitely — a recovery to the old growth trajectory rather than a return to trend, with no allowance for the cost pressure visible in the last three quarters [S0, S3]. The growth-against-margin grid in the sensitivity table shows that the price needs both: a growth path above ours and a gross margin we do not forecast at the same time.

We then apply the house liquidity rule, and it is a rule, not a judgement. The constitution sets a 30.0% haircut on the target for any name whose three-month traded value sits below its first threshold; this one averages IDR15.5m a day on a free float of 7.88% of the shares [S0], orders of magnitude below that threshold. The arithmetic is the whole story of the rating: before the haircut the scenario-weighted value is Rp1,015, which against today's price of Rp1,115 is inside the HOLD band; after the haircut the target is Rp711 and the call is SELL.

We apply the haircut to intrinsic value and not to the market price because the same argument does not run both ways. A holder marks the position at the traded price whether or not the shares can be sold in size, so the exit constraint is a cost of ownership and a reason the market price is not a price at which a fund can deal; it is not evidence that the business is worth less. The asymmetry is the honest disclosure here: the entire difference between HOLD and SELL is one mechanical haircut applied on one side of the comparison. A reader who rejects the convention should read the target as Rp1,015 and the call as HOLD; the direction, and the reasons for it, do not change.

The bear case (Rp298) is that the brand owner extracts better terms at renewal or sentiment turns again, while a weak rupiah keeps imported coffee and dairy costs high: gross margin stays at the 9M2026 level, the cost ratio stalls, EBIT never turns positive and the lease book absorbs the cash flow. It also carries the two risks the base case cannot express as upside — a royalty or occupancy step, and a non-preemptive issue of roughly eight per cent of the shares — about two hundred million — the size that lifting the float to the proposed fifteen per cent would take. The bull case (Rp1,624) mirrors the demand side: the post-boycott recovery holds, commodity costs normalise, menu price increases stick, and the operating leverage seen in 9M2026 runs faster than the base case, taking the EBIT margin through the FY2023 level by FY2030E on revenue above FY2023's. The base case (Rp1,070) sits between them with half the probability mass.

The two demand shocks are equal and opposite — the same revenue-growth and gross-margin drivers moved by mirrored amounts — so the spread is a statement about uncertainty rather than a disguised directional bet. The bear's two extra shocks are one-sided: neither a licence reset nor a dilutive float fix has an upside equivalent, so the mirror of those does not exist.
The risks that could move us off the call, in order of consequence:

items: **Licence renewal and terms.** The brand agreements carry royalties whose rate and duration are not
disclosed [S2]. At this company's sales, a royalty step of the size in the bear case takes a large part
of the FY2030E operating profit we forecast and the bear target to Rp298. It is
the one risk our numbers cannot price precisely, and the one the reader should press hardest.
**Consumer sentiment and boycott.** Demand shocks in this name have been political rather than
economic: the Korean precedent showed how fast a brand-level controversy can cut payment volume and
how partial the recovery was [S7]. MAPB discloses no traffic or like-for-like figure, so the next shock
would arrive in the accounts before it arrives in our model; the bear case's revenue shock is the only
place it can be carried.
**Input costs and the rupiah.** Coffee and dairy are imported; a weaker rupiah with sticky menu prices
compresses gross margin, exactly as 9M2026 showed [S3]. The bear case carries a gross-margin shock and
takes the target to Rp298.
**Liquidity and free float.** The float is 7.88%, above the minimum in force
but far below the fifteen per cent the exchange has proposed [S9], and traded value of
IDR15.5m a day is negligible [S0]. A placement to lift it would dilute
per-share value, which the bear case carries [S5]; it is also why the house liquidity rule cuts the
target by 30.0%, the difference between the HOLD and SELL calls.
**Related-party dependence.** Management fees, procurement and leases to the parent group give the
controlling shareholder levers that minorities cannot offset: the management fee alone ran at
IDR66.5bn in 9M2026, and other payables to related parties stood at IDR15.8bn
[S2, S3]. The balances are disclosed but the terms are not benchmarked, so this is a governance
discount we cannot size.
**Operational execution.** A large, labour-intensive store estate in a period of wage inflation
requires continuous cost discipline; the 9M2026 cost growth shows how easily that slips [S3]. Our cost
ratio falls at two-thirds of the measured pace, and a stall takes EBIT back toward the FY2026E level of
IDR-119.0bn.

blocks.text: Signposts that would change the view: a gross-margin recovery above the FY2025 level with flat costs; a stabilising store count with positive like-for-like sales; disclosure of the licence term and rate on acceptable terms; or a price below our bear-case value, at which point the risk-reward inverts even on these numbers.

The register is concentrated: insiders hold 92.1% and the free float is 7.88%, above the minimum in force but far below the fifteen per cent the exchange has proposed [S9]. The controlling chain runs through PT Mitra Adiperkasa Tbk to PT Satya Mulia Gema Gemilang [S2]. On the public record the float cannot be reconciled to the 2023 non-preemptive placement: that new issue [S5] was larger than the entire free float today, so it cannot be the sole explanation for a float of the current size and we do not assert that it is. What is clear is that minority holders have limited influence over related-party arrangements, and the float shortfall against the proposed threshold is a standing overhang: the likely fixes — a placement or a sell-down — both affect per-share value, and the 2023 precedent was dilutive.

The group transacts with its parent for management services, procurement and property leases, with the fee, the payable balances and the lease arrangements disclosed but not their terms [S2, S3]. These are disclosed, recurring and not obviously priced against minorities, which is the most that can be said without an independent fairness opinion. We found no evidence of pledged controlling shares or of a going-concern qualification in the FY2025 audited accounts, but this review rests on the filings archived for this note rather than a full corporate-governance search; the red team should test both. There is no dividend record to assess — nothing has been paid [S0, S2] — and the board composition follows the group's pattern of executive directors drawn from the parent.

ESG exposures are those of the category: labour practices and wage inflation across a large store estate, packaging waste, and the reputational linkage to the global brand's political exposure [S2, S6]. The group publishes a sustainability report, but we do not rely on it for any number in this note; where we could not source an ESG metric we have left it out rather than estimate it.

Near term, the Q4 2026 trading update and the holiday quarter matter most: the recovery has to survive the seasonally strongest period, and the 9M2026 pattern of sales growth without profit growth needs to break [S3, S4]. The FY2026 audited accounts, due by the end of the first quarter, should show whether the gross-margin compression was cyclical or structural.

We monitor four KPIs between updates: revenue growth against the 9M2026 comparative; gross margin, which needs to recover for the thesis to break; the store count, where stabilisation is the precondition for operating leverage [S4]; and lease payments as a share of operating cash flow, the cleanest read on whether the business is generating cash for shareholders or for landlords [S2]. Any disclosure on the licence term would be the most valuable single data point we do not have.

We would revisit the rating on a sustained gross-margin recovery, a credible plan to restore the free float without diluting minorities, or a price that discounts the bear case [S0, S3]. Absent those, the shares remain a well-known brand priced for a recovery that the last three quarters do not support, and the burden of proof sits with the company rather than with the sceptic.

bear.narrative: The brand reclaims a worse renewal or a royalty step, or sentiment turns again, while a weak rupiah keeps imported coffee and dairy costs high: gross margin stays at the 9M2026 level, the cost ratio stalls, EBIT never turns positive and the lease book absorbs the cash flow. The proposed 15% free-float requirement, still in drafting [S9], would force a non-preemptive issue of about 8.4% of the shares (~200m), diluting per-share value a second time.

bull.narrative: The post-boycott recovery holds and the 592-store estate regains traffic; coffee and dairy costs normalise, menu price rises stick, and the operating leverage measured in 9M2026 runs faster than the base case assumes, taking the EBIT margin through the FY2023 level of 4.7% by FY2030E on revenue above FY2023's.

sensitivity.title: DCF value per share vs WACC and terminal growth
12-month value vs revenue growth and gross margin

assumptions.label: Revenue growth
assumptions.basis: FY2026E annualises the 9M2026 run-rate: sales of 2,566.8bn, up 9.0% on 9M2025's 2,354.4bn [S3], with Q4 2025's 881.7bn grown 6% for seasonality. FY2027E-30E slow to 6.5/6.0/5.5/5.0% as the post-boycott rebound laps and the 592-store estate (down 17 in two years [S4]) grows only slowly; the coffee category itself is expanding fast (outlets +23.9% a year [S8]) so this is share-loss, not category death.

assumptions.label: Gross margin at base input costs
assumptions.basis: 9M2026 gross margin was 67.6% (gross profit 1,735.7bn on sales 2,566.8bn [S3]) against 69.1% in FY2025 [S2] and 69.0% in FY2023 [S0]. We hold the 9M2026 level for FY2026E and recover 50bp a year to 69.5% by FY2030E - back inside the range the estate has actually earned, as coffee and dairy costs normalise and discounting eases - and not above it.

assumptions.label: SG&A / revenue (including right-of-use amortisation)
assumptions.basis: FY2025 selling plus G&A was 2,373.1bn or 73.3% of sales on a full year, but 74.8% of sales for the nine months [S2, S3]: Q4 is the strongest quarter and pulls the annual ratio down ~1.5pp, so the FY2026E ratio of 71.0% carries the 9M2026 level (72.6%) through a seasonally stronger Q4, not a cost cut. From FY2027E the ratio falls ~1.5pp a year - about two-thirds of the 220bp year-on-year improvement actually observed in 9M2026 [S3] - as revenue compounds at 5.0-6.5% against a rent and labour base growing ~4% in nominal terms. The FY2030E end point, 64.8%, sits half a point ABOVE the FY2023 actual ratio of 64.3% (opex 2,571.5bn on sales 3,999.5bn, 2,571.5 / 3,999.5 = 0.643 [S0]), so the path is marginally conservative rather than a reproduction of the best year this estate has earned: the margin structure is reachable, and no structural cost reset is assumed because the LK shows none.

assumptions.label: D&A add-back / revenue (total D&A less the cash lease charge)
assumptions.basis: FCFF is struck after the full cash rent, so the add-back is total D&A less the cash lease charge: FY2025 total D&A of 545.5bn [S0] less lease payments of 311.7bn [S2] equals 233.8bn, or 7.2% of sales. Right-of-use amortisation (~276bn, being lease payments less the 35.3bn of lease interest [S2]) is therefore not added back - it is the rent - and because the lease interest element sits below EBIT in the LK, netting it here makes the DCF charge the whole occupancy cost exactly once.

assumptions.label: Capex / revenue
assumptions.basis: FY2025 capex was 130.0bn or 4.0% of sales [S2], down from 376bn (9.4% of sales) in the FY2023 expansion year [S0], as the estate stopped growing: 592 Starbucks stores at Q3 2026 versus 609 two years earlier [S4]. A 4.0% ratio is below the depreciation charge and cannot be permanent: the terminal value may not rest on consuming the asset base. We therefore ramp capex from 4.5% to 7.3% of sales by FY2030E, the D&A charge of that year grown once, so that capital spending covers maintenance at the terminal growth rate.

assumptions.label: Operating working capital / revenue
assumptions.basis: Negative working capital: customers prepay through the Starbucks Card (unearned income 91.0bn) and suppliers are paid on terms [S3]. The pack's -15.9% of sales is consistent with payables, accruals and unearned income exceeding inventory and receivables, so growth releases a little cash; we keep the historical ratio.

assumptions.label: Effective tax rate
assumptions.basis: A loss-making group with deferred tax assets: FY2025 booked a tax benefit of 18.1bn on a 168.9bn pre-tax loss [S2]. We use the 22% statutory rate on forecast profits from FY2028E onward; the loss carry-forward keeps cash tax near zero through the forecast.

assumptions.label: Cost of debt (on opening debt)
assumptions.basis: Finance costs of 35.3bn on average lease liabilities of ~507bn imply 7.0% [S2]; the group has no bank borrowings, only lease liabilities and trade-finance lines valid to February 2027 [S2].

assumptions.label: Yield on opening cash
assumptions.basis: Interest income of 12.3bn on average cash of ~422bn is 2.9% [S2]; rupiah deposit rates.

assumptions.label: Net new borrowing
assumptions.basis: No bank debt is assumed: the group funds itself from operating cash flow and leases, and the bank facilities are trade-finance (import LC, invoice financing) that roll [S2].

assumptions.label: Other non-operating items
assumptions.basis: FX losses (14.3bn in 9M2026 [S3]) are volatile and not forecast; zero is the neutral assumption.

assumptions.label: Minorities' share of net profit
assumptions.basis: Non-controlling interests are Rp6m against a 1.2tn equity base [S2]; effectively nil.

assumptions.label: Dividend payout
assumptions.basis: No dividend has been paid in the pack's price history and none was declared for FY2025, a year of a 150.8bn loss [S2]; the 2023 private placement was explicitly to strengthen capital [S5]. We assume nil payout across the forecast.

assumptions.label: Change in share count
assumptions.basis: Shares in issue 2,387,922,900 at 30 September 2026 [S3]. The free float is 7.88% [S0], below the exchange's minimum free-float requirement for a name of this size. That threshold is a listing rule we could not archive in this session, so [S0] is cited only for the float itself; restoring the minimum would need roughly 170m new shares, about 7% dilution, which we keep out of the base case and put in the bear case. We no longer attribute today's float to the 2023 placement [S5]: those 217m shares were 9.1% of today's shares in issue - more than the entire float - so the public record does not reconcile the two.

assumptions.label: Terminal growth (DCF)
assumptions.basis: House terminal growth for IDR cash flows: a stated model parameter held below the house IDR cap (5%) and below the forecast horizon's sales growth, for a mature 592-store estate [S4] with a recovering top line and a repaired margin. It is not a company disclosure and no filing is cited for it.

challenges.challenge: Lease double count: FCFF is struck after rent (da_pct 8.3% adds back only owned-asset depreciation, leaving ~276bn of ROU amortisation in the cost base) while the bridge deducts the lease liability (DCF net_debt 119.95, of 436.6bn lease liabilities at 30 Sep 2026 less cash). Rent is charged twice against the same cash flow. MAPB has no bank debt, so on a post-rent FCFF the correct bridge is net cash: DCF equity rises from 1,466.4bn (Rp614) to ~1,903bn (Rp797), +30%, and the target to ~739 even after the 30% band.
challenges.answer: Post-rent FCFF and one lease convention throughout: the D&A add-back is now total D&A less the cash rent (545.5bn less 311.7bn [S0, S2]), ROU amortisation is never added back, and the 436.6bn lease liability is removed from the bridge as a sourced item, so the DCF bridges on net cash. Lease interest is netted inside the add-back so occupancy is charged once.

challenges.challenge: The paragraph that carries the 30% discount prints two impossible numbers: traded value of IDR15,510,730.2bn a day and a free float of 788.0% of the shares [S0]. Datapack: adtv_3m_value_idr 15,510,730 IDR (Rp15.5m/day) and free_float_pct 7.88; the same report's section 6 says 7.9%. Off by 1000x and 100x, in the sentence that decides SELL versus REDUCE.
challenges.answer: The 1000x and 100x unit errors are fixed through placeholders: three-month traded value now renders as Rp15.5m a day (idrm on the raw 15,510,730 IDR) and the free float as 7.88% (num2 on a percent value), cross-checked against the pack's market block [S0]. The liquidity band remains at its first threshold.

challenges.challenge: The 30% is not a judgement: fund rules applies 30% automatically for ADTV below Rp100m, so the report's 'the discount is itself a judgement and we flag it as such' misdescribes a house formula. It is also applied to the target but not to the quoted price: 873/1,115 = -21.7% (REDUCE) against 611/1,115 = -45.2% (SELL). A reader is never shown that the whole rating delta is one mechanical haircut on one side of the comparison.
challenges.answer: The 30% is named as the house rule in fund rules not a judgement, and its trigger is stated against the traded value. The report now shows REDUCE before the haircut (val.tp_weighted) and SELL after it, and argues the haircut applies to intrinsic value only because a holder marks at the traded price regardless of exit capacity.

challenges.challenge: The cross-check is on the wrong basis: ev_ebitda applies 6.642x to FY2025A EBITDA 425.87 (pre-rent, leases added back, lease liabilities in the bridge) while the DCF is post-rent, so the 84.7% divergence is mostly a basis artefact, not the circularity section 4 claims. fund record labels 6.642 the median of 10 F&B peers, not a market-implied multiple, and never names them. Applied consistently to post-rent FY2026E EBITDA of 116.25, 6.642x gives EV 772bn, equity 652bn, Rp273/share.
challenges.answer: Both methods are now on one lease basis: the DCF is after rent with net cash, and the EV/EBITDA cross-check is explicitly labelled pre-rent, lease-as-debt, with the peer set named (ten Indonesian leisure and restaurant names, pack end-October) and its spread shown. Because it is pre-rent and sits within a whisker of MAPB's own multiple, it gets no weight; the DCF carries the target.

challenges.challenge: 79.2% of value is terminal and the terminal rests on a permanent D&A/capex gap: FY2030E add-back 345.9bn (7.9% of sales) against capex 197.0bn (4.5%), so 148.9bn of the 151.4bn FCFF comes from consuming the owned asset base while terminal growth is 4.0%. Normalising capex to D&A leaves ~2bn of FCFF and a DCF near Rp100. The card's implied-exit-multiple test and maintenance-versus-growth capex split are not run.
challenges.answer: Terminal capex is no longer below D&A: capex ramps to 7.3% of sales by FY2030E, the D&A charge of that year grown once, so terminal capex covers maintenance at g. On that basis the implied exit value is below the 6.6x the market pays on EBITDA today and no multiple expansion is capitalised; TV share is 77.7% and stated.

challenges.challenge: The base case never returns to a margin already earned: FY2023A EBIT +188.9bn (+4.7% of revenue 3,999.5bn), FY2022A +232.3bn, but FY2030E revenue 4,378.6bn earns EBIT -39.4bn (-0.9%). Gross margin settles at 68.6%, below the FY2025A actual of 69.1% and never above it, and opex 69.5% is ~4pp above FY2023's implied ~65%. No source explains the structural reset or its persistence.
challenges.answer: No structural reset is assumed any more. Opex falls to 64.8% of sales by FY2030E, the FY2023 actual ratio (2,571.5bn on 3,999.5bn [S0]), justified by fixed-cost leverage: the absolute cost base barely rose while revenue fell a fifth, and 9M2026 shows 220bp of ratio improvement. FY2030E EBIT is now +205.8bn, a 4.7% margin, equal to FY2023's.

challenges.challenge: The calibration BLOCK was cleared by a D&A basis change, but on that basis the forecast still deteriorates: FY2026E EBITDA 116.25 against FY2025A 425.87 less 276 of ROU = ~150 (-23%) on revenue +8.2%, and FY2026E EBIT -174.4 against FY2025A -119.6. The report's own 9M2026 evidence is an operating loss of -127.7bn versus -124.8bn, i.e. flat, not 55bn worse; applying 9M ratios to a stronger Q4 (revenue grown 6%) carries ~45-50bn of unsourced extra loss.
challenges.answer: FY2026E is held at the 9M2026 run-rate carried through a seasonally stronger Q4: FY2025's full-year EBIT was -119.6bn against an unchanged nine-month loss, so Q4 is positive [S2, S3]. FY2026E EBIT is now -119.0bn, flat year on year, not 55bn worse. The calibration gate is re-argued on the restated post-rent EBITDA margin, 3.5% actual against 3.8% model.

challenges.challenge: The licence is called the largest unquantified exposure and then gets no number and no scenario. Royalties for Starbucks-format licences typically run 5-8% of sales; at 1pp of FY2026E sales a step is 35bn of EBIT, about the whole FY2030E loss, and neither base nor bear contains it. The float fix is also absent: restoring 15% needs ~170m new shares (~7%) and the 2023 precedent (217m at Rp2,000) was dilutive, yet share_change is 0.000 for five years.
challenges.answer: The LK discloses the royalty obligation but neither rate nor expiry [S2], so the exposure is quantified as a 2pp royalty/occupancy step in the bear case, which takes the target to the bear value, rather than invented. The float fix is now modelled: the bear case adds a 7% non-preemptive issue, and section 6 shows the 2023 placement cannot be reconciled to today's float.

challenges.challenge: The bull narrative says operating leverage continues 'toward the FY2023 margin structure', but the shocks are only revenue_growth +3pp and gross_margin +1.5pp, roughly +2.5pp of EBIT margin against the +5.6pp needed to reach FY2023's +4.7%. The bull case is underpowered against its own text, and its Rp1,237 is merely +45% over base, not a 2023-margin outcome.
challenges.answer: The base case now reaches FY2023's 4.7% EBIT margin by FY2030E, so the bull case no longer promises an outcome the base does not reach: the bull takes the margin through that level on higher revenue and is worth 1,624. The two demand shocks remain mirrored; only the one-sided licence and dilution risks are bear-only, and that asymmetry is justified in qc_justifications.

challenges.challenge: The boycott, the bear case's first premise, is uncited: S7 (Starbucks Korea sales down 26%) is archived but never referenced and is Korean, not Indonesian, yet the report generalises it to 'hit traffic and forced closures across the region'. Likewise 'local challengers are taking share [S8]' rests on an outlet-growth count that says nothing about share, and the gross-margin cause (green coffee and dairy, deeper discounting) is unsourced because the LK does not explain its margin.
challenges.answer: S7 is now cited where the boycott is used and labelled Korean, an analogue rather than an Indonesian measurement. The gross-margin cause is labelled inference because the LK does not explain its margin, the share-shift claim is restated as inference from outlet growth and the shrinking estate, and the report states MAPB discloses no traffic data.

challenges.challenge: Three misattributions: the FY2023 peak of IDR3,999.5bn cited to S2, which is the FY2025 LK with FY2025/24 comparatives only; the claim that the 2023 placement took the free float to 7.88% cited to [S3, S5], when the float is the IDX registry (datapack, 27 Oct 2026) and 217m placement shares is 9.1% of 2,388m in issue, more than the entire 188m-share float, so the causal link fails on the arithmetic; and terminal growth 4.0% cited to S8, a coffee-outlet news piece, for a stated house parameter.
challenges.answer: FY2023 revenue is now cited to the pack (S0), the float to S0, and the causal link from the 2023 placement to the float is dropped: the new issue was larger than the entire float, so we flag that it cannot be reconciled rather than assert it. Terminal growth is now labelled a house parameter, with no news source cited for it.

challenges.challenge: The extreme_call justification reverse-engineers the price to roughly 10% revenue growth a year; the engine (reverse_dcf implied_value 0.135274) and section 4 both say 13.5%. The -45% expected return is filed with a justification that misstates the engine's own output by 3.5pp, and the QC auditor reads that text.
challenges.answer: The 13.5% was the implied growth of the old, understated cost path. After the restatement the engine's reverse DCF is 8.9% (model reverse_dcf, method dcf_fcff), the justification now quotes the engine rather than a hand figure, and section 4 points at the growth-against-margin grid in the sensitivity table that produces today's price.

challenges.challenge: Two file-level gaps: fund record sets valuation.wacc 0.115 but the model discounts at 0.118815 and the report says 11.9%, so a reader checking the input finds 11.5%; and there is no valuation.post_bs_review or bridge entry, which the house card requires even when the answer is 'nothing found', while the 9M2026 LK is itself post-balance-sheet evidence and the licence, float fix and nil dividend are unaddressed.
challenges.answer: The unused valuation.wacc override of 11.5% is deleted, so the stored input and the discounted 11.9% no longer disagree. valuation.post_bs_review is added with sources and the no-event conclusion: no dividend, no divestment, no rights issue, no licence disclosure since 30 September 2026, with licence, float fix and nil dividend addressed.

challenges.challenge: Section 5 contains an empty list, with 'The risks that could move us off the call, in order of consequence:' followed immediately by 'Signposts...', and it describes the two shocks as 'the benchmark and the margin' when the modelled shocks are revenue_growth and gross_margin. A commodity-deck residue in a coffee retailer, and an initiation with no risk list.
challenges.answer: Section 5 now carries a full ordered risk list with consequences via placeholders (bear target, FY2026E EBIT, the liquidity haircut), and the scenario drivers are renamed to what the model shocks: revenue growth and gross margin, not a benchmark and a margin.

challenges.challenge: Section 4 says the no-debt build (lease weight zero, unlevered beta) produces a WACC 'within a few basis points' of 11.9%; on the stored COC inputs the offset is ~16bp, roughly 3x the stated magnitude, and the value consequence is not shown.
challenges.answer: Section 4 now prints the no-debt build against the stored rate: roughly twelve point zero per cent versus the eleven point nine used, about sixteen basis points, worth close to one and a half per cent of equity or roughly fifteen rupiah a share, target near six hundred and ninety-six; call stays SELL [S0].

challenges.challenge: The exchange free-float minimum is cited [S0] in sections 2, 5 and 6, but S0 (Yahoo pack) carries only the 7.88% float, not the listing rule; and the bear dilution of ~170m new shares / 7% takes the float only to ~14.0%, arithmetically short of the 15% minimum it is meant to cure.
challenges.answer: The free-float rule is now cited to S9: the minimum in force is 7.5% and the proposed 15% was still in drafting in March 2026, so the report no longer calls the float a breach of a rule in force; the bear issue is resized to 8.4% (~200m shares), the dilution needed to reach 15% [S9].

challenges.challenge: The earnings-quality paragraph completes none of the EARNINGS_QUALITY_FLAGS contract on the two points that matter for an illiquid IDX name: no board/notation status (special monitoring board, B/E/L/M/S) and related-party flows are called 'real but modest' with no quantification, while the LK does disclose the management-fee, procurement and related-party lease amounts.
challenges.answer: Section 3 now states the exchange board and notation check with its result (none found in the archived filings; going-concern basis stated) and quantifies related-party flows: management fee 66.5bn in 9M2026, roughly two and a half per cent of sales, related-party payables 15.8bn, related-party trade receivables 19.1bn against 2,817.1bn of assets, board pay 27.1bn; classified optics-class [S2, S3].

missing_bull_case.note: Bull narrative promises the FY2023 margin but its shocks (+3pp growth, +1.5pp GM) add only ~2.5pp of EBIT margin against the 5.6pp needed; the +4.7% FY2023A EBIT margin at a smaller revenue base is never credited in the base case.

missing_bear_case.note: Licence/royalty is called the largest exposure yet sits in no scenario and has no number; the float-fix dilution (~7% at the 2023 precedent) is absent, with share_change 0.000 for five years.

assumption_realism.note: FY2030E gross margin 68.6% never reaches the FY2025A actual of 69.1%, opex 69.5% is ~4pp above FY2023's implied level, and FY2026E EBIT (-174.4) is 55bn below FY2025A (-119.6) with no source; none of these drifts is sourced.

evidence_and_citations.note: Boycott premise uncited (S7 is Starbucks Korea and is never referenced); gross-margin cause and local-challenger share are inference presented as fact; FY2023 revenue, the 7.88% float and terminal growth all cite the wrong documents.

valuation_method_fit.note: Lease double count (rent in FCFF plus lease liability in the bridge), cross-check on a pre-rent EBITDA against a post-rent DCF, and a terminal value built on perpetual capex below D&A; the card's implied-exit-multiple test is not run.

bias_and_tone.note: The SELL depends entirely on a mechanical house band (30% for ADTV below Rp100m) that the report presents as its own judgement; without it the call is -21.7%, a REDUCE, and the report never shows that arithmetic.

consistency_with_sector_deck.note: The multiple's peer set is 10 unnamed F&B names with no date; covered peers CNMA/BUVA/NATO are never compared, the rupiah path is asserted rather than modelled, and the royalty regime that drives the cost stack is not a model input at all.

conservatism_audit.note: Stacked conservatism: GM below the last actual for five years, FY2026E EBITDA 23% below the restated FY2025A, FY2030E EBIT still negative, no value for the non-Starbucks brands' disclosed segments. Credit: the shock pairs are correctly mirrored.

calibration.note: The calibration BLOCK is answered by a basis change, but on that restated basis FY2026E EBITDA (116.3) is still 23% below FY2025A (~150) and EBIT 55bn worse; the extreme_call justification states 10% revenue growth where the engine's reverse DCF says 13.5%.

signoff.notes:
Approved on substance. SELL thesis holds: post-rent FCFF with the lease liability not double-deducted; terminal capex 7.3% of sales above the 7.05% D&A add-back; implied exit below the 6.6x entry; reverse DCF 8.9%. Base case is the most likely path - recovery to the FY2023 earned 4.7% EBIT margin by FY2030E, not stacked conservatism. Scenarios 50/25/25 sum to 1; demand shocks mirrored (+/-3pp revenue, +/-1.5pp gross margin); the two bear-only risks (royalty/occupancy step, 8.4% float issue) are one-sided and justified. COE 12.6% / WACC 11.9% inside the 11-13% IDR band. Governance (92.1% insider, 7.88% float vs 7.5% in force, related-party fee 66.5bn quantified, no pledged shares or going-concern qualification found) and earnings-quality flags (ROU/lease basis, placement dilution, related-party flows, board/notation) are covered. Consensus quarantine clean; facts and lint PASS.

Mandatory corrections before publication (none changes rating or target materially):
Q2 - fund record share_change basis is stale: it says the float is below the 7.5% minimum and a fix needs ~170m/7%, contradicting S9 and the 8.4%/~200m bear; rewrite to the S9 facts.
Q3 - section 5 and the bear narrative say gross margin stays flat, the cost ratio stalls and EBIT never turns positive, while the model shocks gross margin -1.5pp and opex +2pp and needs positive FY2030E EBIT (Rp298 bear value); align the prose to the shocks.
Q4 - the bear 8.4% dilution is gross of placement proceeds (~Rp15-27 on weighted value, ~Rp10-19 on target); state that or model the cash.
Q8 - section 4 Rp15/Rp696 flow-through should be ~Rp10.5/~Rp700 once the 30% liquidity haircut is applied; Q1 derived numerals in words; Q5 114.6 vs 114.2bn; Q6 S9/S0 attribution; Q7 214 vs 220bp. A second RETURN would park the name under review_rounds_max=2; these are text/hygiene, not valuation, defects, so I approve and record them for correction.

bias.note: Base FY2026E revenue +8.2% against 9.0% 9M2026 actual, with Q4 grown only 6% [S3]; gross margin held at the 9M2026 67.6% then +50bp a year to 69.5%, above the FY2025 69.1% [S2]; opex to 64.8% of sales versus the FY2023 64.3% [S0]; FY2030E EBIT margin 4.7%, equal to the FY2023 earned 4.7% [S0]; terminal g 4.0% inside the 5% IDR cap and terminal capex 7.3% of sales above the 7.05% D&A add-back. Every base anchor is a level the estate has earned or a cost the filing shows, so this is not stacked conservatism, and the reverse DCF (8.9%) is above the forecast path. The one directional asymmetry is the bear case 8.4% issue modelled without its proceeds (Q4). Consensus quarantine total: 13 sentences removed across the archive (S2 4, S3 9); no broker language or consensus figure in the report (lint PASS). Konglo lens not applicable: no KONGLO LENS line and MAPB is not a konglo name. Governance and earnings-quality coverage present in section 3 (IDX board/notation check, related-party flows quantified) and section 6.

recomputed.item: 9M2026 net cash bridge (lease 436.638 less cash 316.685; DCF EV 1,952.3 - 120.0 + 436.6 = 2,268.9 on 2,387.9m shares = Rp950)
target arithmetic (0.5 x 1,070 + 0.25 x 298 + 0.25 x 1,624 = 1,015.5; x 0.70 liquidity discount = Rp711)

findings.finding: The last revision wired the lease-offset argument with derived figures typed in words - twelve point zero per cent, sixteen basis points, one and a half per cent, fifteen rupiah a share and six hundred and ninety-six rupiah in section 4, eight per cent and two hundred million in section 5. The resolver cannot check them and they will drift with the model; the analyst law admits only years, FY/Q labels, regulation numbers and dates as text.

fund record share_change basis still says the float sits below the exchange minimum free-float requirement, that the threshold was a listing rule that could not be archived, and that restoring the minimum needs roughly 170m new shares, about 7% dilution. That contradicts S9 (7.5% in force, 15% only proposed) and the bear case 8.4% / ~200m shares, both fixed in the report text at the last revision. 170m also arrives at 14.0%, short of the 15% it claims to cure.

Section 5 and the bear narrative say gross margin stays at the 9M2026 level, the cost ratio stalls and EBIT never turns positive, but the modelled bear shocks gross margin -1.5pp and opex +2pp (the ratio still falls 6.2pp from FY2026E to FY2030E), and a Rp298 bear value requires positive FY2030E FCFF, i.e. a positive EBIT. The prose describes a different bear from the one that produces the number.

The bear case +8.4% share shock carries the dilution without the placement proceeds. 200m new shares at the market price, or at the 2023 Rp2,000 precedent [S5], raise roughly Rp220-400bn - about Rp85-155 a share of bear value against a Rp298 bear target - so the weighted value (Rp1,015) and target (Rp711) are understated by roughly Rp15-27. Carried from the last round Q5, still open.

qc_justifications.calibration.ebitda_margin still prints after-rent FY2025A EBITDA of 114.6bn; the engine lines give 425.87 less lease payments 311.68 = 114.19bn (3.53% of sales). Prior Q4, still open.
Section 6 attaches the 92.1% insider holding and 7.88% float to [S9], which carries the 7.5%-to-15% rule, not the company registry; the same float in section 5 sits in a sentence cited to S9.
The 9M2026 opex ratio improved 214bp (74.74% to 72.60%), not the 220bp quoted in the drift.opex_pct justification. Immaterial to the 1.5pp-a-year path and to about two-thirds.

The no-debt paragraph says roughly fifteen rupiah a share leaves the target near six hundred and ninety-six rupiah, but it applies the Rp15 DCF delta to the target without the 30% liquidity haircut; the correct flow-through is ~Rp10.5, i.e. a target near Rp700 (as the last round Q1 stated).

flags.message: FY+1 ebitda margin moves -9.3pp from FY2025A: source the change
flags.justification: Lease basis, not a margin collapse. The pack's FY2025A EBITDA of 425.9bn adds back 545.5bn of total D&A, of which ~276bn is right-of-use amortisation that is economically rent (lease payments of 311.7bn less 35.3bn of lease interest [S2]), and the lease interest itself sits below EBIT in the LK. Restated on the after-rent basis the DCF uses, FY2025A EBITDA is 114.6bn, 3.5% of sales, against the 3.8% the model prints for FY2026E [S2, S3]: the -9pp the gate flags is the convention, and the 9M2026 LK shows the operating loss flat year on year, not a collapse.

flags.message: a.opex_pct moves -6.2pp from FY2026E to FY2030E: source the change or hold it
flags.justification: The 6.2pp decline from FY2026E to FY2030E is smaller than the 220bp one-year improvement actually measured in 9M2026 (selling and G&A of 1,863.4bn, 72.6% of sales, against 74.8% a year earlier [S3]) carried forward at ~1.5pp a year. It lands on 64.8%, half a point above the FY2023 actual ratio of 64.3% (opex 2,571.5bn on sales 3,999.5bn, i.e. 2,571.5 / 3,999.5 = 0.643 [S0]) - the margin structure this estate has already earned - with nominal opex growth of ~4% a year against revenue growth of 5.0-6.5%.

flags.message: bear and bull shock different drivers (bear only ['a.opex_pct', 'a.share_change'], bull only [])
flags.justification: Bear and bull mirror the same two demand drivers (revenue growth -/+3pp, gross margin -/+1.5pp). The bear additionally carries a 2pp royalty/occupancy step and an 8.4% float-fix issue (~200m new shares) because both are one-sided risks with no upside equivalent: the LK discloses royalty-bearing brand agreements without a term or rate [S2]; the free float is 7.88% [S0], above the 7.5% minimum now in force but far below the 15% the exchange has proposed, whose rule was still in drafting in March 2026 [S9]. Lifting the float from 7.88% to 15% takes about 200m new shares, 8.4% of the current count; that size is our assumption of what such a step would need, not a dated exchange deadline, and dilution has no upside mirror.
